analysis.one_liner: Forces failed-bank executives to return up to five years of pay when their bank collapses.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill requiring failed-bank executives to give back up to five years of pay died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever getting a vote, despite three hearings.
analysis.plain_summary: When a bank fails and the FDIC takes it over, this bill would force executives deemed responsible for the failure to return up to five years of salary, bonuses, stock awards, and stock-trading profits. That money would go back into the deposit insurance fund or the Treasury. It would also make the parent company's creditors and shareholders — not the deposit insurance fund — absorb the losses of a failed bank subsidiary.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary depositors, taxpayers who ultimately backstop the federal deposit insurance system, and the fund itself, which would recover money from the executives who ran failed banks instead of absorbing the losses alone.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Depositors and the deposit insurance fund

how_it_helps.text: When an insured bank goes into FDIC receivership, the FDIC must claw back all or part of the previous five years of covered compensation — salary, bonuses, performance-based pay, equity awards, and profits from buying or selling securities — from any executive or insider responsible for the bank's condition, with the money going to the Deposit Insurance Fund or the Treasury.

The bill extends the FDIC's existing clawback power over executives of large financial companies so it applies regardless of which legal process put the FDIC in charge, closing a gap in the Dodd-Frank statute.
It states that when the FDIC resolves a failed bank, the creditors and shareholders of the bank's holding company must bear the losses, rather than leaving them with the deposit insurance fund.

analysis.who_pays: Executives and other insiders deemed responsible for a failed bank, who would surrender up to five years of compensation, and the creditors and shareholders of failed banks' parent companies, who would absorb losses they currently may not have to.

drawbacks.text: The clawback applies to any institution-affiliated party 'responsible for the condition' of a failed bank, a standard that leaves the FDIC broad discretion and would likely trigger years of litigation over how much fault each executive bears and how much pay to take back.

Requiring holding-company creditors and shareholders to absorb failed-bank losses could raise the cost of raising capital for bank parent companies; banks that face more expensive funding could pass some of that cost to borrowers through higher loan rates.
The bill works only after a bank has already failed, so it does nothing to stop risky behavior before a collapse — it compensates for losses rather than preventing them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and targeted: money clawed back from failed-bank executives goes straight into the deposit insurance fund, and loss-bearing shifts onto investors who chose to back the bank. The main design risks are the vagueness of the 'responsible party' standard, which invites litigation, and modestly higher funding costs for bank holding companies. On balance the bill's costs fall on a narrow, identifiable group — the people who ran failed banks and the investors who financed them — while its protection spreads across the whole deposit-insured public.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee — which held three hearings on related bank-failure matters — but the committee never voted on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
It had bipartisan support: four senators cosponsored it — two Republicans (Josh Hawley and Mike Braun) and two Democrats (Catherine Cortez Masto joining Warren).
The Banking Committee held hearings in May 2023 (with printed hearing S.Hrg. 118-441), but never held a markup or vote on the bill.
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Failed-bank executives and holding-company creditors and shareholders, who would have faced clawbacks and loss-bearing under the bill, are better off because it never advanced; the FDIC and the deposit insurance fund continue to absorb failed-bank losses as before.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was a Democrat (Warren) and half its cosponsors were Republicans (Hawley and Braun of the 49 Senate Republicans), giving it 2 of 49 Senate Republicans and 2 of 48 Senate Democrats in support — but no chamber ever voted on it, so no party split can be measured.

industries.industry: Senior bank executives and bank insiders
industries.note: Executives responsible for a failed bank would surrender up to five years of salary, bonuses, equity awards, and stock-trading profits to the deposit insurance fund. Their financial interest in avoiding this runs directly against the public's interest in the fund being repaid.

industries.industry: Bank holding company creditors and shareholders
industries.note: The bill makes these investors bear the losses of a failed bank subsidiary instead of the FDIC's insurance fund. That is a direct transfer of loss-bearing from a government-backed fund to private investors.

Banks that never fail would owe nothing, but the prospect of clawbacks and holding-company loss-bearing could raise banks' cost of capital and change how they pay executives. Some of that cost could reach customers through loan pricing.
